items.prompt:
# Data Physicalization — Style Prompt

> Real statistics built as real objects: every unit is a countable piece of material (a plate, a block, a coin, a bar) stacked to exact scale on a crafted base, shot like a product in a studio — soft key, long shadows, shallow depth of field, physically based materials. The camera reads a number at the edge of one plate, follows the data as it grows, and pulls back until the chart is an installation.
> References (grammar only): data-sculpture and physical-visualisation practice (one unit = one object, the object is the axis); product and still-life photography (a warm key at a low angle, a cool rim, a seamless sweep); annual-report editorial design (one reading per screen, a source line, a quiet grotesk). Copy none of them; never name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

- **The unit is an object.** One plate, block or coin equals one stated quantity, and the rule is said on screen once ("1 plate = 10 GW"). A heavier material marks every tenth unit, so the stack is its own ruler.
- **Scale is exact.** Heights, counts and areas are computed from the data; rounding is one unit at most and written in the facts. Two series compared on the same base use the same unit.
- **Studio light, real matter.** Metal reflects an HDRI, wood shows grain, acrylic transmits; nothing glows, nothing is outlined, no fake UI.
- **Growth is assembly.** Data increases by pieces being placed, one after another, with weight and sound; it never scales or morphs.
- **The pull-back.** At least once the chart is revealed as a made thing: a dial, a table piece, a landscape of stacks.
- **Every number has a source on screen**: real published statistics (or the user's own figures), credited in frame.

Not Isometric Infographic (no icons, no flat colour coding), not Glass Product Render (the object is data), not Data Storytelling (no paper chart or inked axes), not Dark Tech Keynote (no black stage or neon), not Brick Toy (no toy proportions, no characters).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Pieces**: thin boxes or cylinders instanced in the thousands, each with a few-millimetre random offset and yaw, a ±7 % value change and a hairline gap: that is what makes a stack read as stacked, not as a bar.
- **Material per series**, chosen so two series separate in one glance at thumbnail size: brushed metal against tinted acrylic, pale wood against dark stone, copper coins against paper. A third material (e.g. brass) only for the ruler pieces, shared by every series.
- **Base**: a real-texture slab (wood veneer, stone) with inlaid marks: a tick ring, the series' paths, the labels of categories or years, cut into the surface at the base's own scale, lit with the scene.
- **Rendering**: PBR (transmission for acrylic), an HDRI at low intensity for reflections only, a warm key at 20–35° with long soft shadows, one or two cool rims so metal and acrylic separate from wood at distance; GTAO, physical depth of field, 2× supersampling, a light vignette.
- **Screen space only for type**: readings, verdicts, the source line, subtitles, the title card. Every reading is pinned to its object through the same world → screen function as the camera.
- **Post**: grain light (the background is pale), no lens flares, no chromatic aberration.

## 3. Colour logic

- The set is warm and neutral: a seamless greige sweep, the base in a natural material, the series in material colours (silver, pale teal, brass, oak). Material, not paint, separates series.
- **One accent** (e.g. signal orange) for the reading or verdict that matters on this screen; nothing else is accent-coloured.
- Ink is near-black at two strengths (value, then labels at ~60 %).
- No rainbow series palettes, no colour ramps on the objects, no dark mode.

Example (our demo): sweep #C4BEB4, walnut base, aluminium #C8CCD1 (metal), acrylic #9FD3D6 with teal attenuation, brass #D2B07A, ink #1C1D20, accent #D4521C.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- **Roles**: a light grotesk for numbers (e.g. Inter 200–300; the hero reading 130–170 px, a stack reading 46–56 px); a sans for labels and verdicts in the film's language (e.g. Noto Sans SC 500, 24–46 px); a monospace for units, years and source lines (20–24 px); a serif only for the title. OFL, self-hosted, CJK subset.
- **A reading** = a dot on the object, a 1.4 px leader, a small swatch of the series' material, the category line, then the value and unit, on a translucent paper plate (~84 %). Two readings of one pair stack in one column, larger value on top.
- **The source line** (dataset, publisher, year, licence, e.g. "数据：IRENA (2026)，经 Our World in Data 整理 · CC BY 4.0") is in frame with the data, small (20–22 px, ink at ~60 %) in a corner away from the subtitles, at least from the first reading to the summary, and on the title card.
- **A verdict** sits in the upper-left third on its own plate in the accent colour, underlined by a growing rule; it appears only after the readings it judges have been still for ≥ 2.5 s.
- **Subtitles**: bottom-left, a 2 px ink rule and a paper plate fading right; if the film is bilingual, the film's language on top; each line one line only, measured with the real font (`nowrap`), split into two cues rather than wrapped. Hold ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s).
- Labels hold ≥ CJK characters ÷ 4.5 + 1.5 s / letters ÷ 15 + 1.5 s; a counter reports its landing value; nothing below 20 px.

## 5. Motion quality

- On ones, 24 fps; the camera never stops (2–5 % creep on holds).
- **Cascade**: a stack assembles bottom-to-top in 0.5–1.0 s, each piece dropping a few centimetres with an ease-out.
- **Feed**: one period's increase arrives piece by piece from out of frame, quintic ease-out, a yaw that unwinds ("placed", not "dropped"), 8–16 pieces per second, the counter rolling with the pieces landed.
- **A single heavy object** falls with gravity, lands with one small damped bounce, its shadow tightening.
- Readings fade in with a 16 px rise and draw their leader; they leave by fading, never by sliding.
- Never moves: the base, a piece once landed, the ruler pieces.

## 6. Camera grammar

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Macro dolly along a stack's edge, rack focus | the unit is real and countable | the rule "1 piece = X"; a single record |
| Low lateral track along the series | time passing; growth | a decade; a ranking; a sequence of sites |
| Locked three-quarter frame on two subjects | comparison | before/after; A against B; a crossover |
| Crane with the rising top | accumulation | one year's increase; a target being reached |
| Pull-back to near top view | the whole as an object | a summary; a ratio; an ending |
| Slow orbit around the base | the installation as sculpture | a title; a breath |

The subject fills at least a third of the frame height at key moments; readings live in empty background, never over the subtitle strip; comparisons keep both subjects completely in frame. Transitions are camera moves inside one set (one continuous take where possible); no cuts to a chart, no wipes, no page turns.

## 7. Sound palette

- **The material's own sound** is the foley: metal plates tick bright and short (inharmonic partials 3–8 kHz), acrylic toks duller (1–3 kHz), wood knocks, coins ring. A cascade is a burst of these at the landing times, scaled down as density rises.
- **The ruler sings**: every ruler piece (each 10th) rings a pitched mallet note, one timbre per series (e.g. glockenspiel for metal, glass harp for acrylic), climbing a pentatonic scale with the count — the chart becomes an arpeggio.
- **Score**: mallets and air — marimba ostinato, bowed and struck vibraphone, harp, glass, a soft synth pad and a pulse bass with audible 2nd/3rd harmonics; horns for a turn. Accelerate by subdivision (8ths → 16ths), not tempo.
- **Impacts**: a turn or a last object lands on punch (60–120 Hz) + bass drum + timpani + a bell; the two or three designed impacts are the loudest moments.
- **Silence**: a 0.3–0.6 s suck-out (music and foley −30 dB) before each designed impact; a thin studio-air bed stays.
- **Mix**: voice ~10 dB over music, ruler notes under the voice, −14 LUFS, true peak ≤ −1.2 dBTP. Voice: calm, precise, short sentences.

## 8. Native moves

- **The unit close-up.** Push into the side of a stack until one piece fills the frame; bracket one piece ("= 10 GW") and one ruler piece ("= 100 GW"). *Fits content like:* tonnes of CO₂ as steel plates; a budget as banknote bricks; a population as wooden discs.
- **The paired climb.** Two series on one base, one material each, built year by year as the camera tracks; the crossover is held still with both readings before the verdict. *Fits content like:* imports vs exports; renewables vs fossil capacity; two companies' revenue.
- **The feed.** One period's increase arrives piece by piece onto last period's level, the counter rolling with the landings. *Fits content like:* this year's new hires on last year's team; a quarter's sales; a record harvest.
- **Chart to installation.** Pull back until the bars are a dial, a skyline or a table piece; the base's inlaid marks become its typography. *Fits content like:* twelve months as a clock; regions as a map-shaped base; product lines as a city.
- **The last object.** One single heavier piece (a brass puck, a coin, a weight) lands on the base carrying the final number engraved. *Fits content like:* a total; a ratio; a target met.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- Two materials too alike (bright aluminium vs clear acrylic) read as one series: give one a tint or a finish change, and check at thumbnail size.
- Long shadows and warm reflections turn metal brown at distance: add a cool rim light and keep the base darker than the pieces.
- Thin pieces moiré at 2–3 px per layer: random per-piece value and offset, 2× supersampling.
- A reading pinned to a moving object can leave the frame: clamp it to a safe box.
- Counters that roll by time instead of by landed pieces lie; tie them to the object count.
- Rounding to whole pieces can invert close values; when two values are within one unit, say so on screen or choose a finer unit.
- Transmission streaks at low angles: acrylic roughness ≥ 0.2, tinted attenuation.

## 10. Engine

- `demo/set.js` — `buildSet(scene)` (HDRI, warm key + cool rims, base with inlay canvas, instanced pieces per material, the last object) and the landing schedule (`SHEETS`, `EVENTS`, `landed(stack, t)`); change `PAIRS`, the unit and the materials for any single or paired series.
- `demo/film.js` — cylindrical camera keys (`track`, `core/lib.js`) with focus on a target point, the reading kit (`pairLabels`, `verdict`, `plate`, `swatch`), counter, subtitles (`SUBCHECK`), `TEXTS`, `EV`. `demo/mix.py` — material foley (`tick_alu`, `tok_acr`), ruler notes, suck-outs, master.
- **Extra packages and packs**: beyond `setup.sh deps` only the studio HDRI, `sh tools/fetch.sh hdri` (Poly Haven, CC0, 12 MB); with narration `setup.sh deps voice`; for a sampled score `sh tools/fetch.sh instruments vsco2ce` / `vcsl` / `freepats`. The walnut veneer is in `core/assets/polyhaven/`. Anything you add (a spreadsheet reader, other textures) goes into a private venv / node_modules in the project folder, never into `$LIB/.venv`.
- Minimal example, not in the demo: one series of twelve monthly values on a 12-position circle, the annual total engraved on the last object.

### Sources, licences, facts

- **Statistics for a new topic**: Our World in Data (each chart's "About this data" names the original source; CC BY 4.0 — credit both), World Bank Open Data (CC BY 4.0), Eurostat (CC BY 4.0), US Census / BLS / EIA (public domain); UN Data, IRENA, IEA free tables and other national statistics offices (e.g. 国家统计局): check each dataset's terms. Search the portal for the indicator, download the CSV, keep the file and its metadata in the project's `data/`.
- **Licences**: CC0, public domain and CC BY are fine with a credit. ODbL, CC BY-SA, "no known restrictions" or "free for non-commercial use" are not CC0: name the terms to the user and ask before using them. Textures and HDRIs: Poly Haven / ambientCG (CC0).
- **The user's own numbers** (annual report, ESG data, sales): ask for them and for the document they come from; never invent or round them into a better story. Never let generated images stand in for real data or material.
- **Keep a FACTS.md in the project folder** — each on-screen number and spoken claim, its source URL, the quoted wording or row, and how any derived value (ratio, difference, units per piece) was computed — and deliver it with the film.

## 11. Variation space

Decided per film: the unit and its materials, the base and its shape, which series share it, the camera route, pacing, the last object, accent hue within the colour logic.

- Structures: a single series rising to a record; two series and their crossover; a ranking of regions laid out as a map-shaped base.
- Openings: the macro of one piece being placed; the finished installation seen from above, then the dive to the first unit; an empty base with its inlay waiting.
- Endings: the last object landing at the centre; a slow orbit of the whole installation; a single piece lifted off to show what one unit is.

---

items.prompt:
# Exploded Teardown — Style Prompt

> A real product, built from its own engineering files (CAD, PCB layout, bill of materials), lit like a studio packshot and taken apart in front of the camera: the layers lift on one axis, the camera travels between them, every part is named with the numbers its files contain, and it closes again into one object.
> References (grammar only): hardware-launch exploded films (layer stagger, orbit timing), repair-guide teardowns (opening order, the macro on the part that matters), engineering drawing (leaders, dimension lines). Never copy their products, layouts, typefaces or music, or name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

A frame reads as this style when:

- **the object is real and exact**: geometry, positions and counts come from the product's own files (STEP, KiCad, BOM, assembly guide). Nothing is eyeballed that a file can give;
- **it is shown apart**: layers float on one axis with even, readable gaps, each still oriented as it sits in the product;
- **it is photographed, not drawn**: physically based materials, a studio key light, a cool rim, an HDRI reflection, soft contact shadow on an invisible floor;
- **the numbers live on the object**: thin leader lines from a dot on the part, dimension lines with ticks drawn in the scene's own perspective, never a table beside it;
- **the camera never stops travelling**: one or a few continuous moves, orbit outside, macro inside.

It is not a glass product render (one object, material beauty, no disassembly), not a blueprint (line drawing on a grid, no light), not a keynote (slides, headline type, a stage), not an assembly manual (step numbers, arrows, hands).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- Real-time PBR (three.js `MeshPhysicalMaterial`) at 2× and downsampled, ambient occlusion, a depth of field with one aperture for wide and macro (blur follows 1/focus − 1/z, so it grows as the camera comes close), a high-threshold bloom for emitters only, a vignette.
- Each material keeps its character: plastics with soft sheen (roughness 0.55–0.7), boards with a thin clearcoat and traces as a raised, lighter relief under the mask, metallic pads, tight highlights on machined metal, matte rubber.
- **Boards are painted from their layout files**: copper pours, every trace, via, pad and drill, silkscreen, on both sides, at 14–20 px per millimetre, with roughness, metalness and bump maps from the same drawing. Components stand at their footprint positions with their package sizes.
- Light: a warm key from above front, a cool rectangular rim behind that follows the camera so edges separate from the ground, a soft top light, a low HDRI for reflections; a practical fill only where the camera goes inside.
- Background: a dark graphite seamless sweep (screen-space radial gradient), floor visible only as soft shadow.
- Effects anchored to the world (leaders, dimension lines, glows) are projected from 3D points every frame; only subtitles and title cards live in screen space.

**Where the geometry comes from.** For the user's own product, ask for its STEP / IGES / KiCad / other CAD exports, BOM and spec sheet before anything else. For a public product, look for open hardware (GitHub, GitLab, OSHWA certification list, Hackaday.io, Printables/Thingiverse sources with the original CAD) and component datasheets from the maker. CC0, public domain, CC BY and MIT are fine with credit; CERN-OHL (-P, -W, -S), CC BY-SA, GPL hardware and "no known restrictions" are not the same thing: name the terms to the user and ask before using them. Without files, build only from published dimensions (datasheet, spec page), say on screen or in the voice that it is a model, and show no number you could not source. Never stand in a generated image for the real part.

Keep a FACTS.md in the project folder (claim, source URL, quoted wording, or the measurement method for anything measured from the CAD) and deliver it with the film.

## 3. Colour logic

- The product brings its own colours; the frame around it is neutral and dark, so the product is always the brightest, most saturated thing.
- Interface ink is one warm white at two strengths (names at full, specs at about 60 %), plus **one accent** reserved for measured things: dimension lines, label indices and one matching detail on the product itself.
- Values are ordered: ground darkest, product mid to light, labels lightest. Never put text on a busy, bright part without a dark backing.
- Example (our demo): ground #34363a → #0d0e10, ink #f1efe9, accent #ff6b3d.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- Names: a clean sans at medium weight in the film's script (28–32 px; Noto Sans SC 500 in our demo). Specs and numbers: a monospaced face (15–22 px; JetBrains Mono) so digits line up and read as measurement. A neutral grotesque (Inter) for Latin running text.
- Label structure is fixed: a two-digit index in the accent, the name, one spec line. Units always written (mm, MB, ×n for counts). A label carries at most one fact the voice does not say.
- Dimension text sits on a small dark plate, follows the line's angle and is never upside down.
- Subtitles: a centred strip at the bottom with a soft shadow and no box; if the film is bilingual, the film's language on top. Hold every cue ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s); every label stays fully in frame for CJK ÷ 4.5 + other ÷ 15 + 1.5 s.

## 5. Motion quality

- 24 fps on ones; everything is smooth and deterministic.
- **Separation**: smooth start, fast middle, long settle (ease-in-out cubed); layers leave top first, 0.15–0.2 s apart; repeated parts (keys, screws) fan out in a wave ordered by distance from a corner.
- **Closing**: bottom first, quicker (about 1 s per layer), the last layer lands with a real mechanical response (a key travels its stroke and returns; nothing bounces like rubber unless it is rubber).
- While held apart, layers may float a millimetre or two with offset phases; during macro shots they hold perfectly still.
- Labels draw in (anchor dot, leader growing, text sliding 10 px) and fade out before the parts move again.
- Never moves: the floor, the light rig's relation to the camera, the label column's x position.

## 6. Camera grammar

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Orbit while layers separate | the whole, its order of assembly | a reveal; a structure overview |
| Grazing macro dolly | touch, material, finish | an opening; a texture |
| Dive between layers | being inside | a hidden component; how it works |
| Slow push on one still part | the part that matters | a chip, a sensor, a seal |
| Rise through the stack | one subsystem to the next | a transition between stops |
| Fast pull back | return, synthesis | a closing; a before/after |
| High three-quarter drift | scale and precision | sizes, pitch, thickness |

- At key moments the subject fills at least a third of the frame height. Labels live in a column on the free side (shift the projection with a view offset rather than moving the object), subtitles in the bottom 12 %.
- Transitions are camera moves through the object itself. No cuts to black, no slide transitions, no split screens.
- The camera path is keyed in the product's own coordinates and interpolated without overshoot (monotone cubic), so a held macro really holds.

## 7. Sound palette

- Instruments: tuned mallets (marimba, vibraphone, glockenspiel, glass), a round bass, a short synthetic kick and small dry percussion. Precise and dry outside the object; sustained and airy inside it.
- Foley is the material: hollow plastic clacks for keycaps or housings, a switch click with a low thock, dry taps for boards, inharmonic rings for small machined metal, a soft thud for the enclosure, airy swooshes for layers lifting and for camera dives, a fine pen hiss when a dimension line draws, a tiny tick per label.
- Every separation and every landing has its sound, panned to where the part is.
- Silence: at least two near-silences (room tone only) before the big separations or the turn back; the first sound after each is the most important hit around it.
- Mix: voice clearly on top (music about 10 dB under it while it speaks), music bus ducked, sub-bass kept lean (20–60 Hz well under the full band), loudness −14 LUFS.
- Voice: calm, close, unhurried, short sentences; numbers spoken as words, written as digits.

## 8. Native moves

- **The wave lift.** Repeated parts rise in a wave across the object. *Fits content like:* battery cells; solar tiles; the drawers of a modular shelf.
- **Inside the gap.** The camera enters the space between two lifted layers to see a hidden face. *Fits content like:* the back of a logic board; the inside of a drone arm; the underside of a sensor module.
- **The leader that lands on the part.** A macro label whose line ends on the component. *Fits content like:* a pressure sensor in a shoe; a gasket in a waterproof case; a motor driver.
- **Dimensions drawn on the thing.** After closing, the real outline gets dimension lines in perspective. *Fits content like:* the thickness of a laptop lid; the footprint of a router; the bore of a valve.
- **One real motion.** A part performs its true mechanical motion once (a press, a hinge, a latch). *Fits content like:* a camera shutter; a buckle; a folding hinge.
- **Lights on inside.** Emitters inside the product switch on while it is apart. *Fits content like:* status LEDs; a backlit display; an indicator ring.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- **Invented numbers.** A size that no file gives. Fix: measure it from the CAD and say "measured" in the facts file, or leave it out.
- **Mixed-up revisions.** Plates, cases and boards from different versions of a project. Fix: check hole positions and stack heights across the files (they must coincide), and pin the commit.
- **Panelised boards.** Layout files may hold a panel with breakaway tabs. Fix: take the outline from a plate or case of the same revision, or flood-fill from an interior point.
- **Zero-length edges.** Duplicate outline points give zero normals → NaN → black squares after bloom. Fix: clean outlines, repair zero normals, scan frames for one-frame black tiles.
- **Overshooting camera splines.** Catmull-Rom over unevenly spaced keys flies past a macro stop. Fix: monotone interpolation per component.
- **Labels too short.** Macro stops last about three seconds. Fix: one fact per label, opened before the camera settles; check with `readcheck`.
- **Over-bright light sweeps.** Area lights blow plastics to white. Fix: sweeps at a fraction of the key, bloom threshold above the brightest diffuse surface.
- **Brand marks on parts.** Chip tops and connector shells carry trademarks. Fix: plain package tops; drop logo footprints unless the product is the user's own.
- **Crushed blacks.** Black plastics against a black ground disappear. Fix: lift them to a dark grey and let the rim light separate them.

## 10. Engine

All in `demo/src/` (three.js r170, the library's `core/three/post.js` and `core/lib.js`):

- `parts.js`: `keycapGeometry(w, d, h)` (lofted shell with a spherical dish and a stem), `switchGeometries()`, `loft(rings)`, `shapeFrom(outline, holes, circles)` (KiCad outline to extrusion), `inset`, `hexSpacer`, `screwGeometry`.
- `pcbtex.js`: `paintPCB(data, side, outline, box, ppm)` paints colour, roughness/metalness and bump maps from extracted layout data.
- `comps.js`: `buildBackParts(data, group, y, materials)` places package bodies at footprint positions and returns anchors.
- `overlay.js`: anchored labels (`label`), perspective dimension lines (`dimension`), subtitles, title card, readcheck texts, subtitle width check.
- `main.js`: layers, explode and gap functions, the camera keys (orbit or eye/target, monotone), lights, `window.EV` for the mixer.
- `tools/extract_pcb.py`, `kicad_geom.py`, `sexp.py`: read any `.kicad_pcb` (outlines, tracks, zones, pads, silkscreen, footprints; plain Python). `tools/step2mesh.mjs`: STEP to mesh.

**Extra packages and packs**, beyond `setup.sh deps [voice] [music]`: `occt-import-js` (npm, LGPL-2.1, not in the library's package.json) to triangulate STEP files, and the studio HDRI (`sh tools/fetch.sh hdri`). Install the npm package yourself into a private `node_modules` in the project folder (as `tools/fetch_cad.sh` does in a temp folder), never into `$LIB`.

Minimal example, not in the demo: read a plate file with `extract_pcb.py`, extrude `shapeFrom(outline, cutouts)` 1.5 mm as aluminium (`metalness: 1, roughness: .35`) and orbit it with three `CAM` keys.

## 11. Variation space

Decided per film: which product and revision, which layers to separate and in what order, how many stops inside and which parts deserve them, the camera route, whether to open from the whole or from a detail, the product's palette and the accent, the voice.

- **Three structures**: one orbit with two stops; a "how it works" path following a signal or flow through the layers; two revisions taken apart side by side, each held still before a difference is named.
- **Three openings**: a part performing its real motion in macro; the closed product turning in silence on the seamless; a single component floating alone before the rest of the product assembles around it.
- **Three endings**: closed with its dimensions drawn on it; closing into a top view that becomes a technical drawing; apart one last time, frozen, every part labelled like a printable sheet.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, title card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

items.prompt:
# Microscope Story — Style Prompt

> Real, licence-clean microscopy of a real specimen, seen as it is, and one continuous change of scale that carries the viewer from the glass slide in the hand to a single cell. Focus breathes when the magnification changes, a focal plane sweeps when the camera lands, and every scale bar, field of view and reading comes from the image's own metadata.
> References (grammar only): Charles and Ray Eames' *Powers of Ten* (one continuous change of scale with a readout riding along); premium microscope launch films (dark bench, glass catching light, restrained marks, clean instrument sound); digital-pathology viewers' instruments (scale bar, field of view, magnification). Copy none of their layouts, interfaces, typefaces or music; never name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

- **The specimen is a photograph**: a real micrograph or whole-slide scan of the actual sample, CC0, public domain or CC BY. Nothing on the specimen is drawn, retouched or generated. A whole-slide image (WSI) is the ideal source: one sample, one registered pyramid from millimetres to microns, with the pixel size in its metadata.
- **Scale is the camera**: one log-space dive (and, when the story wants it, the climb back) through nested plates of the same sample. The scale bar shortens and jumps in a 1-2-5 sequence, the field-of-view readout rolls, the magnification steps.
- **Focus has a grammar**: a rack-in from soft at the start, a short breath (blur + a hint of field change) each time the magnification changes, a focal-plane sweep across the frame when the camera lands.
- **Readings are measured**: every number is computed from the file (pixel size × pixels) and the screen says how it was measured. Describe what was measured; never diagnose. Keep a `FACTS.md` in the project folder (claim, source URL, quoted wording, or the measurement method) and deliver it with the film.
- **One reading per screen**, in the single accent colour.

Not Satellite Briefing (no grey grade; the stain keeps its colour), not Sci-fi HUD (no glowing wireframes or crosshairs), not Data Storytelling (no chart paper), not a keynote (no slides or header bars).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Plates**: the WSI pyramid levels as plates in one world frame (level-0 pixels), the coarse levels whole and alpha-feathered at the scan edge, the fine levels as crops around where the camera lands. Each frame draws the finest plate that is downsampled no more than ~1.45×, and blends the next level in between 2.2× and 1.45×: no seams and no visible upsampling, because every level is the same sample, already registered.
- **The naked-eye plate**: the scanner's own photo of the whole slide (many WSI files carry one), registered through the scan's area-of-interest metadata and checked against the tissue's centroid. Cut the glass out of the scanner tray, remove the line-sensor streaks, and fill any manufacturer's printed logo with the surrounding frosted glass. Below ~30 mm of field the photo would be upsampled: let the cover glass become clean glass (its dust leaves the focal plane).
- **One grade for every plate**: glass normalised to a warm white, a little density and chroma in the stain, nothing else. No false colour, no film emulation.
- **The bench**: graphite under a slow pool of light; a soft shadow under the slide.
- **Focus**: screen-space Gaussian blur on a frame rendered with a margin (so edges never go dark); the focal sweep is a tilted sharp front crossing a softened frame. A light illumination vignette, nothing more.
- **Marks** in screen space but anchored to the specimen through one world → screen function: hairlines 1.5–2.5 px with a dark or light halo, circles drawn on as arcs with cardinal ticks, dimension lines with end ticks, leader lines with one elbow. Counted pixels are shown as a mask revealed behind a scan front, then kept as a faint trace.
- **Frosted panels** (dark translucent glass over a blurred copy of the frame) for readings, instruments, subtitles and the credit: white type reads on glass and stain alike, nothing switches colour mid-shot.

## 3. Colour logic

- Glass: warm paper white. Bench: graphite. The stain is evidence and keeps its true colour (e.g. trichrome red and blue, H&E pink and purple).
- One accent, cool and away from the stain's hues (mint against red and blue; amber against a green or purple stain), only for the measured reading and the counted pixels.
- Ink on glass is near-black; type on stain sits on a frosted panel in warm white.

Example (our demo): glass #F4F1EC, bench #0B0D0F → #2A3036, ink #181B1F, panel rgba(12,14,17,0.74), accent mint rgb(120,240,205) (on stain) / rgb(0,122,99) (on glass).

## 4. Type & subtitles

- **Roles**: a light condensed grotesk for readings and the scale bar (40–72 px, e.g. Barlow Condensed); a monospace for instruments and pixel counts (20 px, e.g. IBM Plex Mono); a sans in the film's language for labels (20–34 px, e.g. Noto Sans SC); a serif only for the title. OFL, self-hosted, CJK subset.
- **Instruments** live in one frosted panel in a corner: scale bar with its value, field of view, magnification with a small nosepiece glyph that turns a quarter on every change. The source credit in a small panel in the opposite corner.
- **Readings** sit in a frosted panel beside what they measure, joined by a leader: a small label above ("collagen share of tissue area"), the number large in the accent, the method or the raw counts below.
- **Subtitles**: a frosted strip at the bottom; if the film is bilingual, one line per language with the film's language on top, never wrapped. Measure each line with the real font and split long lines into two cues.
- Nothing below 20 px at 1080p. Hold labels ≥ characters ÷ 4.5 + 1.5 s (CJK); a reading that rolls is reported by its landing value.

## 5. Motion quality

- The camera is a similarity transform (zoom, roll, position) interpolated as a log spiral between keys (M^u about the fixed point of the two frames), so every push is a true dive towards one point and the roll is part of it. Ease the moves, creep 2–5 % during holds; never a frozen frame longer than a second.
- Magnification changes happen where the plates actually change, each with a breath of focus, a turret click and the new magnification said once, large.
- Marks arrive by being made: a dimension line grows from its centre, a circle is drawn as an arc, a scan front counts pixels while the reading rolls, the reading lands with a small spring.
- Never moves: the specimen under its marks, the instrument positions.

## 6. Camera grammar

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| The dive (log zoom with roll) | going to look for yourself | an opening; from the slide to the cell |
| Locked frame, slow creep | evidence, a measurement | a reading; a comparison |
| Truck at one magnification | a second sample of the same thing | the counter-example; "meanwhile, nearby" |
| Pull back to frame two marks | comparison | the verdict |
| Focal-plane sweep | arriving; depth | a landing; a reveal inside one frame |
| The climb (reverse dive, scale bar jumping back) | consequence, scale | an ending; a return to the eye's scale |

At key moments the measured structure fills a third of the frame height or more; instruments in a corner, subtitles bottom centre, readings beside their marks. Transitions are scale changes, trucks and focus, never cuts or crossfades between samples.

## 7. Sound palette

- **Instrument foley**: the objective turret (a click, a detent, a small metal ring), a focus servo, pen on glass for each line drawn, a band-passed scan travelling left to right with counter ticks that speed up, a soft filtered sweep for the focal plane.
- **Music**: hard-mallet vibraphone in 8ths and 16ths, marimba ticks, bowed vibraphone and water glasses for pads and the motif, glockenspiel for each reading that lands, a pulse bass with 2nd/3rd harmonics, timpani and bass drum under the landings. Harmony stays open and light; the score is the user's to shape.
- **Beds**: a quiet lab room (fan, a little mains hum).
- **Silence** before the verdict and before the climb; the first sound after it is the reading or the turn.
- **Mix**: voice ~10 dB over music, music ducked under it; −14 LUFS. Voice: a calm, exact narrator; numbers spelled out for the TTS, digits on screen.

## 8. Native moves

- **The dive.** From the slide in the hand to a cell in one camera, the turret clicking at each real change of level. *Fits content like:* a biopsy to its cells; a coated surface to its crystals; a hair or skin section to its layers.
- **Counting the colour.** Draw a circle, let a scan front cross it, light up every counted pixel and roll the share up to its landing value; show the raw counts underneath. *Fits content like:* collagen in tissue; porosity in a ceramic; coverage of a coating; pigment in a sample.
- **Two circles, one verdict.** Measure one place, truck to another at the same scale, then frame both and say what differs. *Fits content like:* treated against untreated; edge against centre; before against after.
- **The focal sweep and the ring.** Land, sweep the focal plane across the frame, ring one structure and give its size. *Fits content like:* a nucleus; a grain; a fibre's diameter.
- **The climb back.** Pull out to the eye's scale with the scale bar jumping backwards; a title card written on the glass.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- **Licences**: most microscopy on the web is CC BY-NC or all rights reserved. Usable: CC0 whole-slide scans (e.g. the OpenSlide test data: check each file's licence line), public-domain government micrographs (NIH, CDC PHIL, NASA, USGS), CC BY collections (Cell Image Library, Wellcome Collection), with every file listed in `CREDITS`. Not usable: CC BY-SA without agreement, NC images, journal figures, AI images.
- **Finding material for a new topic**: search by organ, stain or material plus "whole slide" in the OpenSlide test data, NCI Imaging Data Commons (TCGA/CPTAC slides, licence per collection), the Cell Image Library, Wellcome Collection, Wikimedia Commons (filter by licence) and NIH/CDC galleries; prefer a file whose metadata carries its pixel size. CC BY-SA, ODbL or "no known restrictions" are not CC0: name the terms to the user and ask before using them. For a product, a lab or a brand, ask the user for their own scans (SVS/NDPI/MRXS, SEM TIFFs with a scale) first. Never stand in a generated image for a real specimen.
- **Different samples never zoom into each other**: two micrographs of "the same thing" at two scales are two specimens. Use one pyramid; if you must join sources, cut on a focus breath and say so.
- **Pixel size**: read it from the file (XMP `ScanRes`, TIFF resolution, OME `PhysicalSizeX`); a slide-photo's resolution tag can be trusted only after checking against the scan.
- **Upsampling** shows as mush beyond ~1.6×: end the dive at the scan's real resolution.
- **Tile seams**: some scanners overlap tiles; check the joint info, frame out visible seams.
- **Labels and logos** on the slide: barcodes and IDs are part of the object; manufacturer logos are not — fill or crop them.
- **Claims**: a stain's colour means what the stain protocol says, nothing more; measured shares are of the drawn region and the stated threshold, never a clinical score.

## 10. Engine

- `demo/film.js`: log-spiral camera (`camAt`), plate selection by downsampling ratio and coverage, objective events from real level changes, focus, frosted `panel()`, marks, readings, `TEXTS` / `SUBCHECK` / `EV`.
- `demo/tools/plates.py`: slide-photo registration and cleaning, graded plates, collagen mask and the scan's cumulative curve, the tissue axis. `nucleus.py`: membrane edge on 72 rays, least-squares circle.
- **Extra packages and packs** (beyond `setup.sh deps voice`): `tifffile` + `imagecodecs` read TIFF-based slides (Ventana BIF, Aperio SVS, Hamamatsu NDPI, generic pyramidal TIFF; `demo/tools/plates.py` is written for BIF: its label page, XMP and AOI); MRXS, SCN, VMS and others need `openslide-python` with the OpenSlide library (`brew install openslide`), or an adapter of your own. Install them yourself into a private venv in the project folder, not into `$LIB/.venv`.
- Minimal example, not in the demo: a coated steel sample: one SEM pyramid, a dive to one crack, a circle counting coverage, a ring around one grain.

## 11. Variation space

The agent decides the specimen, the stain or modality, what is counted, the camera path, the accent, the ending.

- **Structures**: a single dive ending in one measurement; a comparison of two regions or two samples at one scale; a climb that starts on a cell and reveals the object.
- **Openings**: the slide on the bench under moving light; a cell already in focus, the climb revealing what it belongs to; a blurred field racking into focus.
- **Endings**: the title written on the glass; a last reading held in silence; the slide lifted out of frame.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, title card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

items.prompt:
# Archive Light Table — Style Prompt

> Real archive objects (glass negatives, slides, letters, telegrams, clippings, drawings) lie on a cool, backlit light table. A loupe comes down on one of them, and inside the glass the object comes alive: a negative turns positive, a line of type lights up, a number lifts off the page, a photograph opens into depth. Precise catalogue numbers, dates and readings are pinned to the objects. Clean, modern and quiet, with no vintage filter.
> References (grammar only): archive documentaries that push into still photographs; visual investigations that annotate real imagery (one line, one reading, one source per screen); product macro films (glass edges, transmitted light). Copy none of their layouts, typefaces, shots or music, and never name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

- **The objects are real**: scans of public-domain or licensed archive items, at their true proportions, with their real damage (broken corners, emulsion edges, folds, pencil marks). Nothing in them is drawn or generated.
- **Light comes from below**: the table glows a near-white cool grey; film and glass transmit it, paper glows warm at its edges, opaque things read darker than the table.
- **The loupe is the camera's door**: every dive into an object goes through a loupe that lands on it. The inside of the lens is where the object changes state.
- **Catalogue truth**: every object carries its real identifier, date and title from its holder; numbers on screen come from the record.
- **One signal colour** for marks, readings and anchors; everything else is the archive's own greys and paper tones.

**Sources and licences.** Open collections with masters and catalogue records: the Library of Congress (files on `tile.loc.gov`; records from its SRU server `lx2.loc.gov:210/lcdb` when loc.gov pages are blocked), Smithsonian Open Access (CC0), the Rijksmuseum (CC0), NARA, Europeana (check each item's rights statement). CC0, public domain and CC BY (credited) are fine. "No known restrictions", CC BY-SA and other terms are not CC0: name the terms to the user and ask. For brand history, ask the user for their scans, archive numbers and right to use them. Never stand a generated image in for an archive object. Keep a `FACTS.md` in the project folder (claim, source URL, quoted wording, or how a figure was derived) and deliver it with the film.

Not Halftone Dossier (no newsprint dots, no aged-paper grade), not Satellite Briefing (objects on a table, not the ground from orbit), not Data Storytelling (no charts; the numbers live on the objects), not a keynote (no slides or header bars).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **One world, one camera**: every object is a textured quad on the table with a centre, rotation and scale (texture px → world units at true size). The camera is a 2D centre, zoom and roll; the table and every mark go through the same world → screen function.
- **The light table**: an emissive surface (≈ 0.97 white, slightly cool), soft falloff, diffuser noise, an aluminium frame and a dark desk beyond. It can be switched off (ambient ≈ 0.04) and flicker on.
- **Glass negatives**: transmission from the scan's positive, `T = 0.035 + 0.9 · (1 − pos)^1.25`, with a warm silver-gelatin tint; the emulsion mask comes from the scan (white margin touching the border = no glass), so broken corners show the table. Dust and scratches are procedural, anchored to the table.
- **Paper**: backlit, its colour is transmission (paper tone × light); lit lines get darker ink and brighter paper; unlit text can dim to bring one line forward.
- **The loupe**: inside the lens each pixel maps back to the table through the magnification (≈ 2.5×) with a pincushion term (k ≈ 0.16 at the rim), slightly different per RGB channel for colour fringes. Around it: a black ring with a bevel highlight and a clear acrylic skirt that refracts the table and glows at its foot. Landing and lifting, it scales by about 1.35× and casts a soft shadow.
- **The photograph space**: after the push the lens stops being a lens. A photo gains depth from a ground-plane nearness map (zero at the horizon, linear in the row below it), cut-out layers for upright subjects and a filled background; a dolly and a lateral shift drive parallax, and a subject layer may drift. Things left on the ground plane lean: centre the dolly between them.
- **Sampling**: all texture reads inside the branching lens code use explicit gradients (`textureGrad`), otherwise quads that cross a branch pick a wrong mip level and leave dashed seams.
- **Marks** live on a 2D canvas above the picture: hairlines 1.5–3 px, rings, crop corners, underlines, leaders. Table marks are clipped out under the loupe; marks inside a photograph use its forward mapping, parallax included.
- **Post**: a light vignette and fine moving grain (heavier inside photographs). No film damage, no sepia, no halftone.

## 3. Colour logic

- Neutral ground: the light table (near-white, cool) and the archive's own tones (silver greys, paper tans). Do not regrade the archive into a colour scheme.
- **One signal colour** (e.g. a signal orange) for marks, readings, anchors and the verdict; never as a fill behind pictures, never for decoration.
- Text is ink (near-black) on light areas and paper-white on dark caption plates; choose the contrast by the ground, never colour on colour.
- Positives inside the lens may be gently levelled (black and white points) so a weak scan reads; negatives stay as the glass gives them.

Example (our demo): table #F7F9FB, ink #15171A, signal #FF5A1F, caption plates rgba(14,15,17,0.74).

## 4. Type & subtitles

- **Roles**: a monospace for identifiers, dates and readings (e.g. IBM Plex Mono, 17–34 px; readings 74–120 px); a sans for labels in the film's language (e.g. Noto Sans SC or Inter, 21–36 px); a serif only for titles and the one name a photograph carries (60–76 px). OFL, self-hosted, CJK subset when needed.
- **Labels attach to objects**: an anchor dot and ring, a vertical leader, then the text. A reading sits in a dark caption plate with a small label above and the source (the catalogue number or the original wording) below.
- **Subtitles** are a caption strip at the bottom centre, on a dark plate with a 3 px signal-coloured edge. If the film is bilingual, the film's language goes on top. Hold ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s).
- **Quote the source when you can**: a crop of the actual line, or the record's wording in quotation marks, beats a paraphrase.

## 5. Motion quality

- 24 fps on ones; every camera parameter on smooth monotone curves through keys (no overshoot, no stepping).
- The camera glides across the table, slows to let the loupe land, then pushes. Speed lives in the glides and pushes; holds are for reading.
- The loupe lands with a fast ease-out (≈ 0.4 s), lifts the same way. Lines draw on in 0.3–0.6 s; text wipes in from its leader side; numbers count up and land with the voice.
- What never moves: the archive's own content outside a photograph space, and the table itself.

## 6. Camera grammar

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| table glide (pan and roll) | surveying; moving to the next piece of evidence | a timeline of documents; a product family; an album |
| loupe landing + push into the lens | choosing one object; "look closer" | the claim; the key photograph; a signature |
| inside the lens: tracking along a line | reading | a letter, a ledger line, a caption, a spec |
| photograph space: dolly + parallax | being there | the event itself; the founding moment; the place |
| rise out of the lens | stepping back, the evidence noted | a transition; a summary |
| pull back to the whole table | scale; everything at once | an index, a timeline, a closing |

Framing: at a reading moment the subject fills at least a third of the frame height; readings and labels stay clear of the subtitle strip (bottom 140 px). Transitions are made by the loupe (land, push, rise, lift) and the glide; no cuts, fades to black or page turns between objects.

## 7. Sound palette

- **Ambience**: the light table's ballast hum (100 Hz and harmonics), starter clicks, room tone. Inside a photograph the hum gives way to that place's air.
- **Foley**: the loupe on glass (a clack with a high ring), paper sweeps for glides and lit lines, ticks for scales and counters, a pen stroke for a verdict, soft clicks as labels land.
- **Music**: restrained and small: a felt piano, a few strings, glass or bowed metal for the moments of seeing. Build by subdivision and register, not by drums. Leave real silences before a reveal or a verdict; the first sound after them should be the loupe, the place or the verdict.
- **Voice**: a calm narrator, short sentences that state what the object says. Music about 10 dB under the voice, ducked while it speaks; −14 LUFS.

## 8. Native moves

- **Negative to positive under the loupe.** A develop front spreads from the lens centre with a thin warm edge, turning the glass negative into its positive only inside the lens. *Fits content like:* a founder's portrait plate; a factory on a lantern slide; an X-ray film becoming the product inside.
- **The line lights up.** On paper inside the lens one line of type brightens while the rest dims, an underline draws under it, and one word or number lifts out into a reading card. *Fits content like:* a ledger entry; a patent claim; the first order on an invoice.
- **Into the photograph.** The lens rim grows past the frame while the view inside widens; the photograph gains layered depth and a subject drifts. *Fits content like:* the first shop front; a launch day crowd; an expedition camp.
- **Measuring on the photograph.** A ruler laid on the ground plane in perspective, with ticks that crowd toward the horizon and a counter that lands on the recorded figure, marked as a schematic when it is one. *Fits content like:* a race distance; a bridge span; a building's height.
- **Two records, held side by side.** Two caption cards, each with a crop of its source, held still until both are read before one is struck. *Fits content like:* a misprinted date; two versions of a founding story; specification against delivery.
- **The table becomes the index.** Pull back to the whole table; each object's tag flies into one list with its identifier and its reading. *Fits content like:* a company timeline; a collection catalogue; a product family.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- **Over-magnifying a weak scan**: keep the lens interior under about 1.5 screen px per scan px; choose items by scan size.
- **The loupe sweeping over empty table**: lay objects close together, land the loupe straight onto the object (drop in, don't slide in), and glide the camera over objects, not gaps.
- **Shear in the photograph space**: one depth map for a photo with people or machines in it tears them apart. Cut upright subjects into layers, fill behind them, and keep 2.5D moves small enough that the fill is barely seen.
- **Labels that scroll away**: a label on a moving table leaves the frame before it is read; hold the camera, or fix the caption on screen.
- **Vintage creep**: no sepia, no halftone, no paper-ageing overlay. The age is in the objects, not the grade.

## 10. Engine

- `demo/film.js`: `IT` (objects: centre, rotation, scale), `toW()` / `toT()` (texture ↔ world), `CAM` keys and `w2s()`, `dive()` (loupe point, land/lift times, lens interior as tracks), `shot(t)`, `int2s()` (photograph → screen for marks), the shader (`lightTable`, `paper`, `negative`, `parallax`, rim and skirt), the overlay (`annot`, `measure`, `compare`, `indexPanel`).
- `demo/tools/prep.py`: emulsion masks from scans, difference matting of a subject against a smooth sky, ground-only cuts, push-pull fill.
- Minimal example, not in the demo: put one 35 mm slide (`IT.slide = {c, r, k, size}`), a loupe landing with `dive(toW(IT.slide, p), t0, t1, keysS, keysC)`, and light one line with `band()`.
- **Extra packages and packs**: none beyond `setup.sh deps voice music` (numpy, scipy, Pillow, soxr are in the core tier). A score in this palette needs sample libraries: `sh tools/fetch.sh instruments salamander` (piano), `vsco2ce` (strings), `vcsl` (glass, bowed vibraphone). Anything else a film needs goes into a private venv or `node_modules` in the project folder, never into `$LIB/.venv`.

## 11. Variation space

The agent decides the objects, their order, the story, which native moves to spend and where, the camera path, the subject of the photograph space, and the signal colour.

- **Three structures**: a company's founding told as five objects in date order, each dive revealing one person; a single photograph explored in three dives (the place, the people, the date on the back); a before/after pair of plans and photographs of one building.
- **Three openings**: the table switching on in the dark; a loupe already on a plate, rising to reveal the table; a hand-written date on an envelope filling the frame.
- **Three endings**: the index of everything on the table; the last photograph held in depth with one line of text; the light table switching off, leaving one object glowing.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

items.prompt:
# One-line Drawing — Style Prompt

> A single ink line that never leaves the paper. Everything on screen is that one line being drawn; scenes don't cut, they morph.
> References (grammar only): Osvaldo Cavandoli's *La Linea* (1971) — one line is both the world and the character, and transformations of the line are the jokes and the transitions; Gjon Mili's 1949 photographs of Picasso drawing with light — the confidence and speed of a single gesture; Norman McLaren's *Begone Dull Care* and *Boogie-Doodle* — lines drawn *to* the music. Do not copy La Linea's character, its gibberish voice, or any specific continuous-line illustration.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

- **One continuous line** on warm white paper. The pen never lifts: in code the whole film can literally be one point array, from the first touch of the nib to the last frame.
- **Everything is a line**: characters, places, objects, even time. No fills, no shading, no second line weight, no background art.
- **We watch the line being drawn**: the camera follows the nib with a little lag and anticipation.
- Besides ink there is only the paper and a soft **shadow of the pen** (the real world above the paper). One accent colour at most, used once.

Not a whiteboard explainer (no hand, no marker, no erasing, no text-heavy boards), not ink wash (no tones, no brush bloom as a look), not a line-art animation with cuts and many strokes.

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Paper**: warm white (around `#F4EFE4`), procedural mottling (soft-light, large tile), long fibres that fade out when zoomed out (or they shimmer), a sparse paper-tooth speckle over the ink at close zoom, light vignette. All textures anchored to the paper; they move with the camera.
- **Ink** is a filled polygon around the path (not `ctx.stroke`), mixed with paper colour to an opaque tone per point.
  - Width = base width of the current "voice" of the line × pen pressure × fine noise (±8 %); pressure from speed: `0.66 + 0.8·exp(−v/300)` (fast = thin, slow = fat).
  - The line's character can change along the path (base width, alpha, tremble, dryness); blend over a short stretch at boundaries.
  - Ink bleed: the same polygon slightly wider, blurred on an offscreen layer, composited at ~20 %.
  - Pooling: extra round dots where speed drops low.
  - Tremble (perpendicular noise) and dry-brush gaps (long-scale noise + thin bristle strands) for age, fear or fatigue.
  - A stop leaves a teardrop-shaped blot: tip at the nib, belly sagging downward as it spreads, a dark tide line at the rim.
  - **A screen-space minimum width**: widths scale with zoom like a line under a macro lens, but clamp the zoom used for width during pull-backs so a wide view keeps its weight.
- **The pen is never drawn**: a soft blurred wedge of shadow from the nib and a tiny contact dot. Hands, if any, appear only as shadows, each hand composited as one flat layer.
- **Path design**: chapters written as SVG path strings, sampled by arc length, joined by tangent-continuous connectors; time assigned per point weighted by curvature.

## 3. Colour logic

- **Ink on paper.** A warm black (around `#1D1A17`) on warm white; nothing else fills the frame.
- **One accent at most, used once**, on a stretch of the line that means something; it returns to ink afterwards and stays visible in the final picture if the picture is revealed.
- Examples of an accent's job: red for love or danger; blue for water or cold; gold for money or a prize. Never a second accent.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- **Text is written, like the line**: a handwriting face (e.g. Caveat) for subtitles, ink at ~84 %, no box, centred near the bottom, **written on** left to right (~0.2 s + ~17 ms per character) behind a soft paper-coloured halo so passing lines never cross the letters; fade out ~0.45 s. Hold ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s).
- Titles in a monoline connected script (e.g. Sacramento: itself a one-line drawing), written on in empty paper away from the drawing, gone before the camera moves into them.

## 5. Motion quality

- **Everything on ones** (24 fps): the appeal is the continuous act of drawing; stepping breaks it.
- **Timing = chapter windows + curvature**: within a window, time per point is weighted by `1 + K·turn` (sharp turns get more time, smoothed so speed never jumps). Pin musical beats with marks: by arc-length fraction or by position ("the second time the pen passes here"). A stop is two marks at the same place.
- Corners (speed minima at high turn) can be exported to the soundtrack as candidate note onsets.
- Speeds: ~300–700 units/s for travelling lines, ~50–150 for small details. The most important stroke is usually the slowest.
- **Retracing** over an existing line is legal and invisible (it only thickens slightly).

## 6. Camera grammar

A vocabulary, not a route. The camera is one continuous move: composition centre, zoom, a few degrees of roll, and a follow weight (0 = composed, 1 = locked to the nib); the follow point averages the nib over roughly −0.55…+0.4 s (lag and anticipation), with a soft clamp keeping the nib inside the central ~70 % of the frame. Opening and ending come from the topic.

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Follow the nib (high follow weight) | travel; momentum; a thread of time | a journey; a process; a timeline |
| Composed frame, low follow weight | a scene that must read as a whole | a vignette; a joke; a diagram |
| Macro on the nib | intimacy; the act of making | a first touch; a signature; a detail |
| Hold with a slow push-in | weight; a stop | a loss; a doubt; a decision |
| Mirrored framing | rhyme across time | parent and child; before/after |
| Continuous pull-back | everything was one picture | a reveal; a map; a word |
| Lateral scroll with the line running ahead | a horizon; a graph; a race | a stock chart; a heartbeat; a road |
| Roll with the line | vertigo; play | a loop-the-loop; a fall; a dance |

No cuts. Transitions are morphs: the last stroke of one image is the first stroke of the next.

## 7. Sound palette

- **Music: one solo instrument, one unbroken melodic line**, the sound equivalent of the drawing: a bowed or plucked string (cello, violin, viola, harp), a solo woodwind (clarinet, flute, bassoon), a hummed voice, a single guitar. A second colour only as a rare accent (a chime, a pizzicato stretch). No pads.
- **Write the score to the drawing**: key notes on marks and corners; fast line = short notes; a stopped line = one long note fading into silence; the highest note on the most important touch.
- **The pen on paper is the most important sound**, synthesised from the pen speed: band-passed noise (brighter when fast, duller when slow), random paper-fibre ticks with density ∝ speed, amplitude ∝ √speed, panned with the nib's screen position; broken up by dry gaps; lighter and jerkier for a young hand. Plus: a wooden tap on the first touch, a faint wet swell for a blot, a tiny rub for a handoff, a page lift.
- **Silence is literal**: zero the music bus including reverb tails; drop room tone.
- **Mix**: music ducks ~5 dB and the pen ~4 dB under voice; −14 LUFS; grain 0 (the paper is in the render).
- **Voice**: warm, few short lines that leave space for the line; place key words on picture beats with whisper word timestamps.

## 8. Native moves

A menu: use the ones your story needs.

- **The pen never lifts.** Anything that is one continuous thing. *Fits content like:* a river from source to sea; a relay race; a production line.
- **The line is time.** The stroke's character changes with age, mood or strain. *Fits content like:* a building aging; a runner tiring; a machine wearing out.
- **Transformation.** One image morphs into the next. *Fits content like:* a seed becoming a tree becoming a table; a sketch becoming a product; a word becoming its object.
- **Stopping is an event.** The nib stops, ink pools, music cuts to silence (1.5–3 s). *Fits content like:* a power cut; a pause for a minute's silence; a hesitation before a signature.
- **Reverse-designed scale reveal.** Every vignette is secretly part of one big picture seen at the end. *Fits content like:* a city's landmarks forming its skyline; a company's milestones forming its logo; a recipe's steps forming the dish.
- **Handoff.** The pen passes to another hand (as a shadow) and a new line begins. *Fits content like:* a teacher and a student; a founder and a successor; one generation to the next.
- **Line as graph.** The line becomes a chart while staying a drawing. *Fits content like:* a heartbeat; a temperature record; a football match's momentum.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- **Stray connectors ruin a reveal**: every extra line reads as a wrinkle, beard or mask. Fix the topology (where each chapter enters and leaves), not the drawing. Plan it like an Euler path: a closed motif is a circuit (you leave where you came in); retrace or reorder chapters.
- Each region of a final picture is drawn exactly once; connectors must fall on natural lines of that picture.
- **Test the reveal early and often**: render the whole path at once at final scale after every change.
- Lines drawn too close braid together once width is applied; keep a gap.
- A round blot reads as a mole → a sagging teardrop.
- Thin lines at wide zoom → clamp the width zoom.
- Translucent hand shadows double-darken where they overlap → one layer per hand.
- Titles collide with the drawing as the camera moves → check every frame of the title's window.
- Whisper mishears short lines → rephrase rather than fight it.

## 10. Engine

In `demo/`: `geom.js` (samples SVG paths by arc length in the browser, adds tangent-continuous connectors, assigns time by curvature, marks and holds), `ink.js` (the line renderer: pressure, bleed, pooling, tremble, dry brush, accent stretch, blot, minimum screen width), `paper.js` (paper, fibres, tooth, vignette), `cam.js` (composition keys + nib follow + soft clamp), `hands.js` (pen and hand shadows), `subs.js` (written-on subtitles and titles). The drawing itself lives in one file of SVG path strings and a chapter table (`face.js`); replace it with your own path. Debug views (`?all=1`, `?cams=`) render the whole path or many camera views in one session: see [DEMO.md](DEMO.md) "Build notes".

## 11. Variation space

You decide what the line draws, whether it reveals one final picture, where it stops, the accent (or none), the opening and the ending. All far from our demo:

- Structures: **a line that is a graph** (a data series drawn as a horizon; each peak and trough becomes a scene); **two lines** that start in opposite corners and are drawn in alternation until they meet; **a loop** (the line draws a scene and then retraces its way back to the start, which now means something else).
- Openings: **mid-line at speed**, the pen already running across the paper; **a finished drawing** whose line then unravels into the story; **a word written in script** whose last letter becomes the first scene.
- Endings: **the line runs off the edge** of the paper and keeps going; **the ink runs out** and the last stroke fades into dry scratches; **the pen stops in mid-air** over the paper before the last stroke.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

items.prompt:
# Whiteboard Explainer — Style Prompt (v2, no hands)

> An explainer drawn live on one glossy dry-erase board: single-line handwriting that is actually *written* stroke by stroke, floating markers with no hand, magnets that can move, an eraser that can rewind, and a camera that travels across the board instead of cutting.
> References (grammar only): RSA Animate / Cognitive Media (one continuous board, the camera travels instead of cutting, a full-board view); minutephysics (one sentence = one drawing, the simplest geometry that carries the idea); Steve Reich's *Piano Phase* (two copies of one figure at two tempi as a structure). Never copy their drawings, characters, hands or music.

Suits explainers of 60–120 s, usually science or "how does X work".

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

- **One physical whiteboard.** Everything the viewer learns is drawn in dry-erase marker in front of them, in real handwriting order.
- **The board is a map**: each idea lives in its own region; the camera travels between regions, often led by the pen. Distance on the board = distance in the argument.
- **Real marker, not animated text**: ink pools where the nib lands, dry streaks and speckle, strokes overshoot and don't quite close, ghosts of old lessons remain, a glossy sheen drifts slower than the board, and **every stroke makes a sound**.
- **No hands.** Markers float with a real cast shadow that grows when they lift, park outside the frame between phrases and fly back in. Magnets and the eraser move on their own. Never draw a hand, an arm or a cursor.

Not Blueprint (no blue sheet, no drafting conventions), not Crayon Picture Book (no wax texture, no children's story), not a kinetic-type explainer (text is handwritten stroke by stroke, never animated as blocks).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Board**: a warm white gradient, a faint scuff and micro-scratch tile, a few dozen **ghost marks** (old words, circles, arrows) at 5–10 % in grey or pale blue, and a soft diagonal **window sheen** (white, 10–16 %) moving at ~0.35× the camera: this one detail sells "glossy".
- **Ink**: alpha ~0.94, composited with **multiply** so overlaps darken like real marker. Width 6–11 px for drawing, ~13 % of cap height for lettering.
- **Stroke character**: resampled every ~0.6 × width; low-frequency hand wobble along the normal (a few px, long wavelength) plus a finer tremor; chisel-tip width modulated by direction; a pressure ramp at the start and a small taper at the end; circles start at an angle and **overlap past closure**; rectangles are four strokes with small corner overshoot; a darker pooled dot *inside* the start of long strokes.
- **Dry-marker texture**: a speckle-and-streak tile subtracted from the ink layer (destination-out), locked to board space, faded out when the camera is wide.
- **Lettering**: a single-line (single-stroke) font written in stroke order, each glyph with small rotation, baseline and scale jitter. Missing symbols (μ ≈ → × − ✓ ² ° ±) are hand-defined.
- **Props**: dry-erase markers (white barrel, colour band and cap in the ink colour, felt nib), a felt eraser, magnets (glossy, with specular highlight and soft cast shadow). Frame, tray and wall appear only if the camera ever goes past the board edge.

## 3. Colour logic

- **Three marker colours at most**, each with a meaning held for the whole film: one dark ink for things and structure, one for signals / measurement / process, one accent for the thing that matters (one accent per region).
- **Monochrome variant**: everything in the dark ink, one element in the accent (the "only colour").
- Ghost marks and board stay neutral; the accent never appears on props except its own marker cap and the hero magnet.
- Example sets: black `#23262c` / blue `#2a5cb3` / orange `#d97757`; black / green `#2e8b57` / red `#c8363a`; navy `#1f2a44` / teal `#1f8a8a` / purple `#7a4fb3`.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- **Handwriting only**: a single-line hand (e.g. EMS Tech, OFL) for all board text; titles large (~120–200 px cap height), labels 30–70 px.
- **Title and end card are written on the board** in the same hand.
- **Burned subtitles**: an off-white rounded label (~90 %), a handwriting-like face (e.g. Architects Daughter ~44 px), dark text, a short accent-colour marker dash. Split at clauses, ≤ 44 characters per line, bottom ~12 % of the frame kept free for them in every shot. Hold ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s).
- **Writing finishes on the word**: a term appears exactly when the narrator says it.
- A label is fully in or fully out of every shot it appears in.

## 5. Motion quality

- **Hand speed**: every stroke follows a slow-fast-slow curve (`u − sin(2πu)/2π × 0.8`). Strokes are scheduled into a **time window** and the engine solves the speed, so writing always finishes on time.
- **Pen hops** between strokes lift in proportion to distance (shadow slides and blurs); long gaps send the pen off-frame to park and back shortly before its next stroke.
- **Magnet**: drop with a shrinking shadow; slide with a small lift; lift-off and sink possible.
- **Eraser**: constant speed along a path, a wide band at ~90 % strength (a ghost always remains).
- **Speed**: faster than real hands (a sped-up lesson) but never so fast the stroke order is lost: a label ~0.3–0.8 s, a title ~3 s.
- Camera on ones with real motion blur when it moves fast.

## 6. Camera grammar

A 2D camera over a large board (e.g. 8000 × 4500): position, zoom interpolated in 1/z so pushes feel like dollies, a little roll. A vocabulary, not a route. Opening and ending come from the topic.

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Pull back from a tiny drawing | scale | a surprising size; context |
| Ride the line the pen is drawing | one idea leads to the next | a transition; a process; a path |
| Hold still | read now | an equation; a definition; a list |
| Whip to a new region | a new idea after a pause | a twist; a "but" |
| Return to an earlier region | a callback, for free | reusing a result; a comparison |
| Split view of two regions (zoomed out enough for both) | two things at once | a duet; before/after |
| Slow push into one symbol | this term is the point | a unit; a variable; a name |
| Track along a long diagram | sequence, time | a timeline; a pipeline; a journey |
| Pull back past the board edge to the wall | the whole lesson as one picture | a summary; a scale jump |

Motion blur: when the camera moves more than ~14 px per frame, render and average sub-frames (≤ 4 px apart). No cuts on the board; if a cut is needed, it is a whip.

## 7. Sound palette

- **Every stroke sounds**: band-passed felt-on-gloss noise (a hiss band ~2–7.5 kHz + body ~0.5–1.5 kHz) enveloped by the stroke's own speed curve, a tiny nib tick at the start, stick-slip grains, and on some long strokes the **dry-erase squeak** (a 1.5–2.6 kHz sine with 7–13 Hz vibrato). Each colour sounds slightly different. Pan = the stroke's screen x; closer camera = louder.
- **Props**: magnet on steel = click + metal modes + a low board thump; eraser = felt rub modulated by its zig-zag; cap off/on; marker tray bounce.
- **Room**: low room tone; a single diegetic ticker (a wall clock, a fridge hum, a projector fan) can own a silence.
- **Music** options: a solo piano figure; a small jazz trio with brushes; plucked strings and kalimba; a synth arpeggio for tech topics; clockwork minimalism (marimba, pizzicato, woodblock, glockenspiel). Mickey-mouse details: a rising whistle for growth, pings for signals, a harp run for a fall.
- **Techniques to pick from**: adding one instrument per step of a mechanism; a key change when the frame of reference changes; a full stop into silence before a surprise; the previous cue reversed and squeezed for a rewind; two copies of one figure at two tempi (phasing) for anything that diverges, snapping into unison when resolved.
- **Mix**: voice on top (compressed, light room), music well under voice and ducked further under speech, foley ~11 dB under voice; −14 LUFS.

## 8. Native moves

A menu: use the ones your story needs.

- **Writing in stroke order.** The reveal is the explanation: a formula term by term as it is spoken. *Fits content like:* compound interest; the Drake equation; a recipe's ratios.
- **The pen leads the camera.** Transitions are drawn lines the camera rides. *Fits content like:* a nerve signal; a supply chain; the water cycle.
- **Magnets.** The only things allowed to move on a board: give the hero to a magnet; slide, lift, drop, sink it. *Fits content like:* a delivery truck on a route; a cell in a bloodstream; a player on a pitch.
- **The eraser rewinds.** Wiping a trail backwards reads as undoing time. *Fits content like:* an undo in software; reversing a chemical reaction; "what if we hadn't…".
- **Two pens at once.** A live duet comparing two quantities. *Fits content like:* two savings plans; two runners; a population vs its food supply.
- **Ghosts of the old lesson.** A faint previous drawing becomes relevant. *Fits content like:* a theory replaced; last year's forecast; a first draft.
- **The full-board view.** Every region seen at once as one picture. *Fits content like:* a system diagram; a history; a map of a field.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- **One pen, too many jobs** drifts later and later → give each drawing a deadline window and let overlapping jobs go to another pen.
- **Minimum stroke duration × many dashes** makes a dashed line take seconds → dashes need their own floor.
- **A pooled-ink dot bigger than the stroke start** leaves halos on every letter → keep it inside.
- **Punctuation vanishes** (a font period is a 1 px stroke) → render sub-width strokes as dots.
- **Labels half-cut by a push-in** look sloppy.
- **Motion blur with few sub-frames** strobes text.
- **Eraser paths** crossing labels you want to keep.
- **Voice and phoneme set mismatch** (a British voice with US phonemes) mispronounces → match the language code to the voice; ASR-check.

## 10. Engine

`demo/engine/wb.js`: hand-drawn shapes (`line`, `curve`, `poly`, `arc`, `circle`, `rect`, `arrow`, `dashed`, `hatch`), `text()` in writing order from a single-line font (`loadFont`), `Stroke`, floating `Pen`s, `Timeline.draw(pen, shapes, t, {by})` (solves hand speed to a deadline), `Timeline.erase`, `Timeline.cue`, keyed `Camera`, `Board` (ink multiply, dry texture, erasers, sheen, props), prop drawers. API table and a minimal example that draws something new: [DEMO.md](DEMO.md#engine-reference).

## 11. Variation space

You decide the topic's object, the board layout, the colours within the logic, the voice, the music family, the camera route, the opening, the ending and the length.

All far from our demo:

- Structures: **a proof** (one claim at the top, the board fills downward step by step, each step boxed when proven); **a debate** (two pens, two halves of the board, each drawing its side until the drawings meet in the middle); **a timeline** (one long horizontal line ridden left to right, with events hanging off it).
- Openings: **a question mark** drawn huge in the centre, then shrunk to become a dot in the first diagram; **an erased board** where the ghost of a wrong answer is still visible; **a magnet dropping** onto an empty board with a clack.
- Endings: **the answer circled** twice and the pen capped; **the board wiped** except for one line that survives; **a push into the smallest symbol** on the board, which becomes the title.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.
